## Overview

### About the data

The **Health Cost Repository (HCR)** is an interactive, systematic evidence map of published economic data for **malaria, dengue and chikungunya**. It is maintained by the [Modelling and Simulation Hub, Africa (MASHA)](https://science.uct.ac.za/masha) and is intended to help researchers, policymakers and programme planners identify relevant cost studies and locate their original sources.

The repository brings together publication details, study context and information about how costs were reported. It can support searches for evidence on intervention delivery, diagnosis and treatment, household costs and economic burden. This page uses malaria studies for the map, charts and costing example. The intervention matrix compares all three diseases.

Each database row describes a publication. Follow its source link for the numerical estimates, costing methods and study context. One paper may report several costs for different populations, interventions or perspectives.

### How studies are selected

The repository draws primarily on journal articles and technical reports identified through disease-specific searches of **PubMed and Scopus**. Its documented search round was conducted in **August 2026**, combining disease terms with terms for costing, resource use, economic burden and economic evaluation. Identified publications were screened, deduplicated and data were extracted using a standardised extraction form.

### Accessing the data

1. Open **Database** and select a disease, such as **Malaria**.
2. Refine the selection by country or WHO region, intervention, cost collection time frame, publication type or type of cost data.
3. Search the table, select a study title to read its authors and abstract, and open **Notes** for additional costing context.
4. Follow **Reference** in the Source column to the original publication.
5. Use **Download Table → Excel workbook** for analysis or **Word document** for a readable study list.

The **Visualisations** tab provides a separate **Download Summary Data** workbook containing publication records and chart summaries. Its filters include disease, evidence type, cost data source and publication year. Use this workbook for publication summaries and the Database export for the costing details of individual studies.

Save the export date and filters with each download. When comparing totals across tabs, match the evidence-type selection. Visualisations defaults to **Individual studies**, and the Database can also include evidence syntheses.

### What the data looks like

The two workbooks contain the following kinds of information.

| Information | Examples of fields | How it helps |
|---|---|---|
| Publication details | Study title, author and publication year, study design, source link | Locate the publication and understand its design. |
| Costing context | Cost collection period, base year of reported costs, reported currency | Assess the age and monetary basis of the estimates. |
| Study context | Study setting, target population, notes | Check relevance to the population and delivery setting being modelled. |
| Evidence classification | Disease, country, intervention, evidence type, type of cost data | Explore coverage using the Visualisations export and repository filters. |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Data dictionary: terms that are easy to confuse"}

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Publication year | The year the article or report was published. |
| Date of cost data collection | When the underlying cost data were collected. This may be a period rather than a single year. |
| Time frame | The grouping used to filter cost collection periods in the database. It is not the publication year. |
| Base year of reported costs | The price year in which the publication expresses its costs. It may differ from both collection and publication years. |
| Reported currency | The monetary unit used by the source. US dollars and purchasing-power-parity international dollars are different measures. |
| Evidence type | Individual studies versus evidence syntheses, such as systematic reviews and meta-analyses. |
| Type of cost data | Primary data collected by the researchers, previously collected secondary data, or both. This does not mean financial versus economic costs. |
| Not Specified | The database record has no value for that field. Check the source paper for further detail. |

:::

### Key points to consider

- **Unit of evidence:** count publications separately from cost estimates. Multi-country and multi-intervention publications can contribute to several categories; reviews may include studies also listed individually.
- **Comparability:** assess the intervention, delivery setting, population, perspective, cost components, currency, price year and denominator before comparing or combining estimates.
- **Transferability:** an estimate from another country or programme may require adjustment or may not be applicable. Document why each source is suitable for your question.
- **Reporting versus quality:** the presence of a base year or currency helps interpretation but does not establish methodological quality. Review the original methods and limitations.

### Citing and reusing the data

Cite HCR, record the date accessed and cite the original publication for each estimate used. Include the table or page number so another modeller can trace the input to its source.

## Visualisations

### Exploring the evidence landscape

In HCR, the **Visualisations** tab lets you explore study locations, publication years, interventions and sources of cost data. Selecting a country on the map or a cell in the disease-by-intervention matrix opens the corresponding publications in the database.

The map, country table and bar charts use **11 malaria publications** from an HCR export prepared on **9 November 2026**. The selection covers **individual studies** published in **2021–2024** with **Primary** selected as the type of cost data. The disease-by-intervention matrix uses a second export covering all three diseases. A paper covering several countries or interventions contributes to each relevant category.

To reproduce the malaria examples, save both workbooks in the page’s `data/` folder and run the code from the page directory in Health RADAR. The summary workbook comes from **Visualisations → Download Summary Data**. The Database workbook contains the costing fields for the same publications. [Download the example summary workbook](data/hcr-summary.xlsx) · [Download the matching study records](data/hcr-studies.xlsx)


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-summary="Show how to read the example workbooks"}
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readxl)
library(ggplot2)
source("../../../theme_health_radar.R")

summary_file <- "data/hcr-summary.xlsx"
publications <- read_excel(summary_file, sheet = "Publications") |>
  filter(Disease == "Malaria") |>
  distinct(Disease, `Study ID`, .keep_all = TRUE)

# The Database export also contains the source URL for each publication.
studies <- read_excel("data/hcr-studies.xlsx") |>
  semi_join(publications, by = "URL")
```
:::


### Where is malaria cost evidence represented?

The map shows the African countries covered by the selected publications. Grey countries have no matching publication in this export. Studies from India and Myanmar also appear in the workbook.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-summary="Show country map code"}
library(sf)
countries <- read_excel(summary_file, sheet = "Countries") |>
  filter(Disease == "Malaria")

africa <- rnaturalearthdata::countries50 |>
  filter(continent == "Africa") |>
  left_join(countries, by = c("adm0_a3" = "ISO3"))

ggplot(africa) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = Publications), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.25) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#a6cee3", high = "#08519c", na.value = "grey88",
                      breaks = scales::breaks_width(1)) +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(-26, 59), ylim = c(-36, 38), expand = FALSE) +
  theme_health_radar() +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), axis.title = element_blank(),
        panel.grid = element_blank())
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![African countries covered by the selected malaria cost studies.](health_cost_repository_files/figure-html/fig-hcr-country-map-1.png){#fig-hcr-country-map fig-alt='Map of Africa showing four publications covering Nigeria, three covering Uganda, and one or two each in six other countries.' width=720}
:::
:::


The Elimination 8 (E8) countries can also be read as a table. Mozambique and Zambia both appear in the same multi-country study, which is counted once in each row.


::: {#tbl-hcr-e8 .cell tbl-cap='Publications in the example export that cover each E8 country.'}

```{.r .cell-code  code-summary="Show E8 country table code"}
e8 <- tibble(Country = c("Angola", "Botswana", "Eswatini", "Mozambique",
                         "Namibia", "South Africa", "Zambia", "Zimbabwe"))
e8 |>
  left_join(countries, by = c("Country" = "Country Name")) |>
  transmute(Country, Publications = coalesce(Publications, 0)) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|Country      | Publications|
|:------------|------------:|
|Angola       |            0|
|Botswana     |            0|
|Eswatini     |            0|
|Mozambique   |            1|
|Namibia      |            0|
|South Africa |            0|
|Zambia       |            1|
|Zimbabwe     |            0|


:::
:::


### When was the evidence published?

Use publication year to describe when papers appeared. For the age of the underlying costs, use the collection period and price year recorded in the Database.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-summary="Show publication year code"}
publication_years <- publications |>
  count(`Publication Year`, name = "Publications")

ggplot(publication_years, aes(factor(`Publication Year`), Publications)) +
  geom_col(fill = theme_health_radar_colours[8], width = 0.65) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = scales::breaks_width(1)) +
  labs(x = "Publication year", y = "Publications") +
  theme_health_radar()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Publication years of individual malaria studies in the example export.](health_cost_repository_files/figure-html/fig-hcr-publication-years-1.png){#fig-hcr-publication-years fig-alt='Four papers were published in 2021, three in 2022, three in 2023 and one in 2024.' width=672}
:::
:::


### Which intervention categories are covered?

The summary workbook groups interventions into broad categories. The study of seasonal malaria chemoprevention used in the Modelling tab appears under **Prevention**. The **Publications** sheet retains the more specific intervention label for finding that study.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-summary="Show intervention coverage code"}
interventions <- read_excel(summary_file, sheet = "Interventions") |>
  filter(Disease == "Malaria")

ggplot(interventions, aes(Publications, reorder(Intervention, Publications))) +
  geom_col(fill = theme_health_radar_colours[1], width = 0.65) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = scales::breaks_width(1)) +
  labs(x = "Publications", y = NULL) +
  theme_health_radar()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Publications by HCR intervention category. A study may contribute to more than one bar.](health_cost_repository_files/figure-html/fig-hcr-intervention-coverage-1.png){#fig-hcr-intervention-coverage fig-alt='Five papers address prevention and five address case management. One each addresses health system strengthening and social and behavioural change.' width=720}
:::
:::


### Which interventions have cost studies across the three diseases?

Read across a row to compare the number of publications for the same intervention. For example, the **Case Management** row contains 26 malaria publications, four dengue publications and two chikungunya publications. A zero means that no publication in this selection matched that disease and intervention. In HCR, selecting a cell opens its studies in the Database.

For this matrix, the HCR filters were **All diseases**, **Individual studies**, **All cost data types** and publication years **2016–2025**. The counts come from the **Interventions** sheet of the summary workbook exported on **9 November 2026**. Save the CSV in the same `data/` folder to reproduce the figure. [Download the matrix counts](data/hcr-disease-interventions.csv)


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-summary="Show disease-by-intervention matrix code"}
coverage <- read.csv("data/hcr-disease-interventions.csv") |>
  mutate(Disease = factor(Disease, levels = c("Malaria", "Dengue", "Chikungunya"))) |>
  complete(Intervention, Disease, fill = list(Publications = 0))

ggplot(coverage, aes(Disease, reorder(Intervention, Publications, FUN = sum))) +
  geom_tile(aes(fill = Publications), colour = "white", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(aes(label = Publications, colour = Publications > max(Publications) / 2)) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#edf6fb", high = "#083b82", guide = "none") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "#173853", "TRUE" = "white"), guide = "none") +
  scale_y_discrete(labels = function(x) stringr::str_wrap(x, width = 22)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_health_radar() +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Publications by disease and intervention among 43 selected studies. A publication can appear in more than one intervention row.](health_cost_repository_files/figure-html/fig-hcr-disease-interventions-1.png){#fig-hcr-disease-interventions fig-alt='Matrix of six intervention categories for malaria, dengue and chikungunya. All three have case management and prevention studies. Surveillance, monitoring and evaluation has two malaria publications and one dengue publication.' width=720}
:::
:::


## Modelling

### Costing seasonal malaria chemoprevention in Mali

How much would it cost a programme to deliver four monthly rounds of seasonal malaria chemoprevention (SMC) at fixed distribution points? A programme can estimate this by multiplying the number of children reached in each round by the cost of reaching one child in that round. HCR helps identify a study with the right delivery method, population and costing perspective.

### Find a matching study in HCR

In **Database**, select **Malaria**, **Mali** and **Seasonal Malaria Chemoprevention** under **Prevention**. Open the reference for **Diawara et al. (2021)**. The same paper can be found in the example workbooks by matching the country and intervention, then using the source URL to retrieve its costing fields.


::: {#tbl-hcr-smc-study .cell tbl-cap='Costing details for the Mali SMC study identified through HCR.'}

```{.r .cell-code  code-summary="Show how to find the study in the exports"}
smc_studies <- publications |>
  separate_rows(Country, sep = ",\\s*") |>
  filter(Country == "Mali",
         grepl("Seasonal Malaria Chemoprevention", `Category of Intervention`)) |>
  inner_join(studies, by = "URL", suffix = c("", ".database"))

smc_studies |>
  select(Study = `Author (Year)`, `Collection year` = `Date of Cost Data Collection`,
         `Price year` = `Base Year of Reported Costs`, Currency = `Reported Currency`) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|Study          |Collection year |Price year |Currency |
|:--------------|:---------------|:----------|:--------|
|Diawara (2021) |2014            |2016       |CFA, USD |


:::
:::


The authors measured provider costs for a 2014 campaign in Kita that offered SMC to children aged 3–59 months. Their Table 5 reports an **economic cost per child reached per round**, in **2016 US dollars**. That unit matches the programme’s monthly reach. The table also reports a cost per child reached in all four rounds, which uses a different denominator. [Diawara et al. (2021), Methods and Table 5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7934250/#Tab5)

### Apply the published costs to programme activity

First, check the calculation against the study itself. Both the numbers reached and the four unit costs below come from Table 5. A child reached in two rounds contributes once to each round’s cost.


::: {#tbl-hcr-smc-rounds .cell tbl-cap='Provider economic cost by round, reconstructed from the published unit costs and numbers reached in Kita. Amounts are in 2016 US dollars.'}

```{.r .cell-code  code-summary="Show the costing calculation"}
rounds <- tibble(
  Round = 1:4,
  children_reached = c(98790, 104477, 108659, 105093),
  usd_per_child = c(0.92, 0.85, 0.82, 0.85)
) |>
  mutate(round_cost = children_reached * usd_per_child)

rounds |>
  select(Round, `Children reached` = children_reached,
         `USD per child` = usd_per_child, `Cost (USD)` = round_cost) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = c(0, 0, 2, 0), format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


| Round| Children reached| USD per child| Cost (USD)|
|-----:|----------------:|-------------:|----------:|
|     1|           98,790|          0.92|     90,887|
|     2|          104,477|          0.85|     88,805|
|     3|          108,659|          0.82|     89,100|
|     4|          105,093|          0.85|     89,329|


:::
:::


The four reconstructed costs sum to **US$ 358,122**. The authors report **US$ 357,494** for the campaign. The small difference comes from multiplying by unit costs rounded to cents. [Diawara et al., Table 5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7934250/#Tab5)

For a planning example, suppose the programme expects to reach **100,000 children in each of four rounds** using the same delivery approach. Replace the activity counts with that plan and retain the study’s unit costs.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-summary="Show how to cost a planned season"}
planned_reach <- rep(100000, 4)
planned_cost <- sum(planned_reach * rounds$usd_per_child)
```
:::


The estimated cost of that season is **US$ 344,000 in 2016 prices**, assuming similar delivery conditions and average cost per child. It values the resources used, including staff time. For a cash budget, use the study’s financial costs. For a different delivery method, price year or scale of operation, update the unit costs as well as the number of children reached.
